rows.evidence: Q1: Methodology and Results sections - the authors develop their own procedure (maximum/minimum system head curves, 4,000 daily random demand curves, SOLVER-based pump selection) and apply it with their own model runs to a 127.7 ha citrus on-demand network in Valencia (Table 2, Figs. 8-17, Table 4).
rows.notes: The study is a design/optimisation methodology for dimensioning and regulating a pumping station in an on-demand network. It reports simulated design discharges (Cl<U+00E9>ment 166 L/s vs 218 L/s from DRDC maxima vs 256 L/s absolute maximum), a failure distribution function (Fig. 10), and annual total costs (project plus energy) of pump combinations (Fig. 15), concluding that one or two variable-speed pumps plus fixed-speed pumps give the lowest total cost. It does not compare the investment cost of on-demand networks with that of other delivery schedules, nor does it test that higher investment cost arises from guaranteeing supply in peak periods; it only shows that dimensioning for maximum DRDC discharge gives a larger design discharge than Cl<U+00E9>ment's formula. All results are model outputs on design data with no comparison to measured network or cost data, so under the rating rules they do not count as own evidence on the claim. Q9: the study gives standard deviations of simulated discharges and energy (Fig. 8, Fig. 14) but these are not dispersion of the claimed cost effect; set to no because Q2 is no.

notes: Full text appears complete (pp. 273-281). The paper is a simulation/optimisation study applied to one real network but not validated against observed data; it is cited here for a general statement about on-demand network investment cost that it does not directly test.
